The combination of audience and purpose that determines the texts we encounter is what Markel calls the 'writing situation'.

Keeping language clear, simple, and to the point is a core value of technical communication, because readers are trying to do something else and simple language reduces their effort and the risk of misunderstanding — especially where readers are in a hurry, stressed, or not native speakers.

Improve the clarity and simplicity of technical texts by using simple declarative sentences instead of complex ones and by giving clear, simple instructions in chronological order or in a logical cause-and-effect structure.

Scientific texts use simple language only to a degree; because they aim to create an effect or elicit a response rather than merely convey information, they employ a broader range of linguistic devices, including longer, more complex sentences and figurative or vivid language.
condition: scientific and popular-science texts

statement: Metaphors are a valuable tool in both scientific and technical texts: they put a concrete name to an abstract concept and explain complex processes and systems by drawing on readers' existing knowledge (e.g. Black Hole, Greenhouse Effect, Double Helix; worm screw; Trojan Horse; handshake).

Specialized terminology makes up only a small proportion of a technical text — Newmark estimated 5–10% — though the share varies by text and can reach up to about half the word count in cases such as patent extracts.
exception: text types such as patent extracts, where terminology can approach 50%

statement: Technical texts contain highly specialized abbreviations and acronyms whose meaning may vary depending on the subject, the context, or even the company or organization that produced the text.

Beware specialized terms that pose as general terms: ordinary-looking words (such as 'jumper' or 'handshake') carry specific technical meanings that depend on the context and subject area and can be mistranslated if read as everyday vocabulary.

Some information can only be conveyed effectively as bare facts and figures rather than in prose; technical texts tend to present specifications as bullet lists or tables without textual padding, whereas scientific texts present the same hard facts within sentences.

Authors refer readers to information elsewhere — laws, directives, and standards in technical texts; books and journal papers in scientific texts; diagrams, interface items, menus, or accompanying documents in software — to avoid impeding the flow of information or overloading the reader, and documents may be split into smaller ones.

References serve rhetorical functions: scientific references reinforce arguments and convince the reader of the validity of the information and the trustworthiness of the author, while references to standards and laws in technical texts can also signal that a product is reliable and safe by conforming to a standard.

Graphics and illustrations (diagrams, graphs, schematics, photographs, screenshots) are a key feature of technical texts, especially consumer-facing and instructional documents and software, where showing a picture of what users should see on screen is far more effective than verbal description.

A document that contains screenshots is inextricably linked to the external software interface: for the text to be coherent it must accurately reproduce the text shown in the interface, all textual references to the software must be phrased consistently and accurately, and any change to the software requires corresponding changes to the document.

Formulae, equations, and scientific notation let abstract scientific and technical concepts be expressed clearly and concisely, with scientific notation compactly presenting figures too large or small to write conveniently in decimal form.

Numbers rarely appear in isolation; they quantify a physical quantity via units of measure, most of which are governed by the International System of Units (SI), whose seven base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela, each modifiable by prefixes such as micro-, milli-, nano-, and pico-.

Although metric measurements are becoming the international norm, Imperial units (inches, feet, pounds, ounces) still appear in some languages, particularly English, and in text types such as workshop manuals, specifications, and parts catalogues, so a translator should watch for the unit system in use.
Formulae are more compact than any verbal description, accurate because there is no room for interpretation of words, and widely regarded as virtually universally intelligible.

Equations are understandable across languages because each is accompanied by a list or brief paragraph identifying, defining, and assigning a value to every symbol (often introduced by 'where X equals Y'); provided the symbols are clearly identified and explained, the translator must preserve those symbol definitions intact.
Most scientific and technical texts can be grouped under recurring types: manuals, applications and proposals, reports and scientific papers, presentations, regulatory documents, and popular science.

A website is a communication medium and distribution channel rather than a text type of its own; document types persist even as they adapt to the web, and documents that were once printed (manuals, brochures) are increasingly distributed only electronically.
Manuals are educational tools whose aim is to give the reader easy access to precisely the information they need at a particular moment and to ensure it is clear and comprehensible.

Procedural (cookbook-style) manuals consist of a bullet list of prerequisites and a numbered list of steps, are best suited to procedural information broken into discrete stages, and require the flow of information to be controlled so the reader is not overloaded.
condition: procedural, step-based documents

statement: It is bad practice to combine multiple tasks into a single sentence no matter how elegant the sentence is; when a source sentence crams several tasks together, the translator may need to split it into separate ordered steps so the reader immediately knows what to do and in what order.
condition: instructional or procedural text

statement: Tutorials introduce a topic or product gently in stages and must be encouraging and supportive and avoid confusing, too-advanced, or wrong information, because most people (about 63% in one study cited by Schriver) blame themselves for problems they encounter following instructions even when the text is clearly substandard.
condition: tutorial documents

statement: Not all tutorials target complete novices; for transfer users who already understand allied technologies, the translator need not explain every concept but must avoid over-simplifying the text so much that these readers feel patronized.
condition: tutorials aimed at transfer users with prior related experience

statement: Tutorials present information at a slow pace with low information density, and they help readers avoid mistakes — which in Europe is also a legal requirement, since directives require product documentation to alert users to potential hazards caused by incorrect use.

Guides follow on from tutorials and teach more advanced material to readers who already have a basic understanding; they contain plenty of examples — which translators may need to adapt to the target-language culture — alongside detailed descriptions, figures, tables, and diagrams.
condition: guide documents for readers with basic prior knowledge

statement: When a single document combines a tutorial and a guide, its function usually shifts from instructional to explanatory after the first few chapters as the reader gains understanding, so the translator must change translation strategies accordingly partway through.
condition: documents combining tutorial and guide functions

statement: Reference manuals are comprehensive documents for knowledgeable readers refreshing details; their material is organized into focused, independent topics (alphabetical or logically grouped) that are dipped into rather than read cover to cover, so certain information may need to be repeated across topics to prevent readers skipping back and forth.
condition: reference-manual documents

statement: Where cross-references are used, the names of the referenced topics, sections, or documents must be accurate and consistent; if another translator has handled or will handle the referenced section, the translator must liaise with them to ensure both use identical wording (a translation memory tool will auto-suggest the wording only for sections the same translator has already done).
condition: documents containing cross-references

statement: Automatically generated reference manuals compiled from programmers' notes and code comments risk containing poor or unclear writing of inconsistent standard, because programmers are not trained writers.

Online help is accessed in situ within software and comes as general (searchable) or context help; it consists of task-based, hyperlinked, discrete and independent topics with an unpredictable entry point, so each topic should be readable quickly, ideally on a single screen without scrolling, using short, simple sentences.
condition: online help systems

statement: A proposal is a complex request composed of subtexts (abstract, biographies, cover letter, project description, schedule, budget), each with its own function, content, and style; rather than one strategy for the whole document, the translator should apply a single macrostrategy for the document supported by local microstrategies for individual sections.
condition: documents composed of heterogeneous sections such as proposals

statement: Scientific papers and reports follow a small number of standard structures, chiefly IMRAD (Introduction, Materials and methods, Results, Discussion) or the fuller Abstract, Introduction, Materials, Procedure, Results, Conclusions, References.

An abstract, together with the title, must function as a text in its own right so potential readers can decide whether to read the paper; a translator cannot leave anything awkward or unclear in an abstract on the assumption it will become clear later, because the ambiguity may stop the reader from continuing.
condition: abstracts of papers and reports

statement: In the Materials section of a paper, correct spelling and orthography are essential because it often contains proprietary or trademarked names.
condition: Materials section of scientific papers

statement: In the Procedure section, consistency and absolute clarity are required and there is no room for inaccurate or unclear information, because errors can affect the repeatability of an experiment and render the study unreliable; watch especially for abbreviations, acronyms, units of measure, and ellipsis.
condition: Procedure/methods sections of scientific papers

statement: The Results section is an objective statement of facts with no discussion; where it includes reported speech from interviews, the translator should translate exactly what is written, as it is written, even if it does not make perfect grammatical sense.
condition: Results sections containing reported speech or interview data

statement: A journal's stipulated bibliographic style (Harvard, MLA, APA) is not the translator's to change, but when translating between different scripts (e.g. Chinese to English, Russian to Arabic) the translator should decide, or ask the client, whether to transliterate author names and book titles so the target audience can read them, using an ISBN to find any official gloss or transcription.
condition: reference lists, especially when source and target use different scripts

statement: A case study is a primarily marketing text that combines technical-report content with marketing and journalistic language to show the benefits of a technology or a company's expertise, and it follows a fairly standardized format: identify the client, explain its needs (the 'problem'), describe the solution and its implementation, a testimonial section, and closing company descriptions with contact details.

Case studies are demanding to translate because they use a broad range of writing styles to convey different information — highly complex technical data together with subjective personal opinions, reported speech, and persuasive devices.

A well-constructed presentation is highly summarized and consists largely of bullet points rather than paragraphs of text, which means the slides are potentially ambiguous and often make complete sense only when accompanied by the spoken presentation.
To resolve the ambiguity of presentation slides, the translator should where possible ask the client for clarification or, better, for the speaker's notes or the full version of the paper.
condition: translating presentation slides

statement: When translating presentations, watch translation length: because text boxes do not auto-resize, a translation longer than the source is shown in a smaller font that can become illegible when projected or spill off the slide, and the translator should not add a new slide without first checking with the client about slide-count, timing, or design limits.
condition: translating presentation slides

statement: Regulatory (normative) documents are explicit sets of rules — essentially specifications — that give clear, comprehensive, and unambiguous descriptions of what a product must do, what characteristics a material must have, or how a service is to be provided, and take formal shape as directives, laws, or standards written by bodies such as ISO, DIN, or BSI.

Regulatory documents usually have a legal dimension (enforcement, justification, or prevention) and so overlap with legal translation, carrying legal terminology and constructions alongside detailed technical descriptions; patents in particular protect intellectual property by giving the inventor the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the invention.
Translating regulatory documents requires meticulous attention to detail to ensure factual accuracy and, at the same time, compliance with specific linguistic requirements imposed on the document.
condition: regulatory and normative documents

statement: For medicine product information, the European Medicines Agency's EMEA templates define the required format, layout, and wording and stipulate specific headings, spellings, and established phrases across many languages; product information must conform to them exactly or the medicine may be withdrawn, and because they exist in many languages they double as a ready-made, approved terminology resource for translators.
condition: medicine product information subject to EMEA templates

statement: Popular science presents scientists' observations, data, and conclusions in an accessible way to entertain and educate a general audience, so much of the modality and cautious hedging present in scientific texts is often absent because of the need to simplify or generalize principles.
condition: popular-science texts

statement: Popular science is hybrid, combining scientific terminology, abbreviations, and equations with literary or journalistic features and even unusual devices (dialogues, storytelling, metaphors, cartoons), so it can be particularly demanding to translate.

The structure of technical documentation is not random: it is shaped by the function of the text, the circumstances in which it will be used, a logical progression of topics, and cultural preferences and norms — so understanding why a text is structured a certain way helps decide the most appropriate translation strategy.

Some texts are written in a linked, cohesive way where each section builds on the previous and leads into the next (e.g. popular science books, specifications, proposals, textbooks), while others are composed of more or less discrete sections designed to be read individually in no particular order (e.g. reference manuals, task-based tutorials, troubleshooting guides, online help).

When translating texts made of discrete, independently read sections, avoid anaphoric and cataphoric references (pointing backward or forward to content in other sections) because readers may find them unclear or unfamiliar; instead make the reference more specific (name the chapter) or repeat the necessary information and delete the reference.
condition: texts with discrete sections read in unpredictable order

statement: Hybrid texts display features of more than one text type and may jump between scientific, technical, marketing, financial, legal, and promotional writing (as in proposals, tenders, reports, case studies, and marketing material), so the translator must recognize the change in function of each section and adapt translation strategies accordingly.
condition: hybrid or multi-function documents

statement: Recognizing a text as a sample of a particular type is essential, because without the ability to recognize its form one could neither comprehend, write, nor translate it (Bell 1991); a knowledge of cross-cultural similarities and differences in genres and conventions is therefore crucial to the translator (Schaffner 2000).

Genres are embedded in socially determined communicative activities: some are highly culture-specific and vary significantly across cultures while others are supra-cultural or universal, but even where conventions are ostensibly universal, individual languages require different micro-level strategies (for example, giving instructions uses imperative verb forms in English but infinitive forms in German).

Titles and headings serve identifiable functions (Nord: distinctive, metatextual, phatic, informative/referential, expressive, appellative); a title should be translated to conform with target-culture convention, which may mean converting an expressive source title into a purely informative one.

Gopferich's pragmatic classification groups technical text functions into juridical-normative, progress-oriented (actualizing), didactic-instructive, and compilation categories, providing a framework for understanding what a given text type is meant to achieve.

Many everyday scientific and technical text types fall into the didactic-instructive category, whose target audience is highly heterogeneous and therefore poses the greatest number of translation problems, making thorough audience analysis especially important for these texts.
condition: didactic-instructive texts with heterogeneous audiences

statement: A scientific paper is a written report of original research whose purpose is to inform and persuade peers as to the validity of the observations and conclusions and the effectiveness of the methods used.

The abstract, together with the title, must be self-contained because they are published separately from the paper in abstracting services, where they let a reader identify the paper's content quickly, judge its relevance, and decide whether to read it in full.
condition: abstracts of scientific papers

statement: Many abstracts are written by the authors themselves, who may be non-native speakers of the language of the abstract, so abstracts may be fraught with language errors that the translator should expect and handle rather than reproduce blindly.
condition: abstracts written by non-native-speaker authors

statement: The precise challenges facing a translator vary with the nature of the text and especially with the language combination and direction: what poses a problem in one target language may pose none in another.

Create a document profile for a text type — identifying its subject, audience, text function, key features, and potential problems along with strategies for dealing with them — as a methodology for preparing to translate that text effectively.

A technical data sheet (TDS) provides detailed product information on a product's composition, properties, and applications together with product safety, legal considerations, and environmental issues, and its precise content varies with the product, the company, and the legal requirements of the countries of production and sale.

Test instructions are essentially a type of standard operating procedure (SOP) that gives clear, step-by-step explanations of how to carry out inspections, and typically form part of a comprehensive reference set accessed as needed.

Expert technical reports are a common text type for technical translators, associated with engineering disciplines; they provide details of the object of study, the circumstances surrounding the test, and the materials and methods used, and are often produced by highly qualified specialists in an independent, consulting role.

A user guide provides instructions to help users learn how to use a product, using explanations, examples, advice, and logical, structured procedural information that takes the user through each step, supported by simple, uncomplicated language and graphics, tables, and boxes to aid learning.

User guides aim at usability grounded in (theoretically universal) human cognition, yet they also contain features that make them acceptable to specific cultural groups and are rarely aimed at a single group or culture, so translating them is not always straightforward.

Popular science serves as a bridge between scientists and the general public, aiming to make findings accessible and to convey their significance and implications; to do so it sometimes simplifies concepts or states information as fact where a scientific text would be more tentative, so a translator should be aware the source may overstate certainty relative to the underlying science.
condition: popular-science texts

statement: Document profiles for the sample text types can be created by the translator as an analytical exercise, and Appendix 4 supplies reference sample profiles; the more detailed a profile's identification of key features and potential problems, the better the translator understands how to approach that text.

A European Certificate of Conformity (COC) is a manufacturer's declaration that a product conforms to the relevant European regulations, intended to ensure the free movement of goods within the EU; it contains product and producer identification, a type-approval number, and applicable technical specifications, with content defined by EU regulation but varying by product or service.

A technical case study is a marketing text that combines technical language with marketing and journalism to promote products by giving a real-world applied context and presenting a very positive client experience; its language must reflect that positivity without overstating or misrepresenting the reality of the product.

A technical case study normally follows a set structure: a catchy headline and a quote or testimonial summarizing the client's experience, then the client's business activities and needs (the 'problem'), then how the company helped (the 'solution'), supported by interview quotes, diagrams, and statistics.

The basic translation strategies used in scientific and technical translation are not unique to it; they are used across all types of translation, and this book shows how they apply specifically to scientific and technical texts.

Vinay and Darbelnet distinguish direct translation — straightforward strategies requiring less intervention and less deviation from the source text — from oblique translation, which is used when the grammatical, pragmatic, and lexical differences between source and target language are too significant to allow direct translation.
The direct translation strategies are literal translation, borrowing, and calquing; though linguistically unsophisticated, they are useful in a range of scenarios.

Literal translation is more sophisticated than word-for-word replacement: begin translating word by word but switch to group-by-group or clause-by-clause once the target text stops complying with target-language grammar, reflecting the source's content and features as closely as possible and deviating only enough to keep the target grammatically correct and intelligible, while avoiding additions, omissions, and paraphrasing.

Literal translation is one of the most frequently used strategies in technical texts — more frequent than transposition, modulation, addition, or adaptation (Cardoso de Camargo) — yet it covers a smaller proportion of the words in technical texts (about 39.6%) than in journalistic texts (about 45.3%).

A literal translation can be grammatically, syntactically, and idiomatically correct from a purely linguistic point of view yet still be inappropriate in the target text, because different audiences have preferences and expectations about how information is presented to them.

Borrowing transfers a source-language lexical item into the target text without modification (except transliteration for different scripts); it is used when the target language has no existing word or concept, or deliberately to create a foreign or exotic effect, such as evoking the source culture in a popular-science text.

Calquing literally translates the constituent parts of a source word or phrase to create a target-language neologism; it should be approached with caution because a calque can sound alien and a neologism may confound readers, so new words should not be introduced without good reason where acceptable target-language alternatives already exist.
exception: when there is genuinely no acceptable existing target-language alternative

statement: Oblique translation (Vinay & Darbelnet) comprises four procedures — equivalence, transposition, modulation, and adaptation — used where the stylistic or linguistic features of the source text make a straightforward replacement of elements produce a target text unacceptable in meaning, structure, idiomaticity, or style.

Equivalence as a procedure replaces source elements with target elements that replicate the same situation using completely different wording; it is used for fixed expressions, formulaic phrases, idioms, and proverbs, and in technical texts specifically for translating warning signs and labels (e.g. 'Danger!' rendered as 'Risk of Death').

Transposition (recategorization) replaces one class or type of word in the source with a different type in the target without changing the meaning; it is needed when keeping the same word class would be awkward or unintelligible, and can be obligatory or optional (chosen for style or flow) — examples include turning a nominalization into a verb, a passive into an active, or a passive into an imperative.

Modulation changes the form of information by presenting it from a different point of view; it is useful where a literal translation would be grammatically correct but unidiomatic, and includes shifts such as positive to negative, abstract to concrete, part for whole, and adopting a target-language-preferred viewpoint. Some modulations are compulsory (structural) and some are free.

Adaptation is a strategy of last resort — the extreme limit of translation — to be used with caution; it applies when the source describes a situation or concept that does not exist in the target-language culture or lacks the same connotations or relevance, and it uses three procedures: cultural substitution, paraphrasing, and omission.
condition: when a source concept has no equivalent or the same relevance in the target culture

statement: Apply adaptation in order: first try cultural substitution (replace a source-culture reference with the corresponding target-culture one); if that fails, paraphrase the meaning descriptively; and only if both fail, omit information — and then only as a last resort that you can fully justify, because technical documentation is concerned first and foremost with information.
condition: adapting culture-specific source content

statement: Paraphrasing is perhaps the most useful procedure for technical translation because, beyond resolving culture-specific problems, it helps avoid interference and unidiomatic constructions caused by sticking too closely to the source text.

Expansion (exploitation) makes something implicit in the source explicit in the target — adding explanatory phrases to clarify terms or connectors to improve flow — to make the target clearer, more relevant, or to compensate for the target audience's lack of background knowledge; it may raise semantic redundancy, which technical texts tolerate well because they are explanatory by nature.

Use expansion to improve cohesion and coherence when the source was written by an untrained writer (excessive jargon or ellipsis), when the target audience has less subject or background expertise than the source audience, or when the source audience is high-context but the target audience is low-context and expects information spelled out.
condition: target audience needs more explicit information than the source audience

statement: Contraction (removing unnecessary detail) may be needed when the target audience already has the background knowledge, but the decision to add or omit detail carries a two-sided risk — patronizing one audience with obvious instructions or forcing another to guess by omitting them — so it should be driven by the target audience's expectations.
condition: when source and target audiences differ in background knowledge or cultural preference for detail

statement: Contraction makes something less detailed in the target text to fit the perceived expectations and background knowledge of the target audience, and can also be used to eliminate information that is reasonably unnecessary, irrelevant, or potentially confusing for that audience.
Recycling information is a way of clarifying a text by expanding a translation using information already provided elsewhere in the same text.

Generalizing makes source information less detailed in the target text by omitting information or replacing a specific term (hyponym) with a less specific one (hypernym); it is useful when the target language lacks a similarly specific word or when a specialized text is being translated for a general audience unfamiliar with the specific term.
condition: target language lacks the specific term, or a specialized text is aimed at a general audience

statement: Generalizing works only if the specific term is not essential for comprehension, can reasonably be inferred from the context, or can be reintroduced elsewhere in the text; otherwise the original specific information must stay, or the reader will not fully understand or be unable to act.
exception: when the specific term is essential and cannot be inferred or relocated, it must be retained

statement: Particularization (specification) uses a more specific term than the source's, needed when the source's generic term is too broad in the target language, introduces ambiguity, or carries undesirable connotations; it requires understanding the subject well enough to choose the correct specific term (e.g. does 'motor vehicle' mean car, truck, van, or motorcycle?), so good communication with the author or client, or access to a subject-matter expert, is vital.
condition: source generic term is too broad, ambiguous, or carries unwanted connotations in the target language

statement: Over-translation and under-translation can be deliberate strategies but can also happen accidentally to the detriment of the target text — for example rendering 'fuel' as the narrower 'petrol' in an EU safety directive introduced a wrong, more specific meaning with potential safety, financial, and legal consequences — so a translator should ensure a target term carries the same connotations and denotational meaning as the source term unless there is a valid reason to do otherwise.
exception: when there is a valid, deliberate reason to broaden or narrow the meaning

statement: Compensation makes up for the loss of certain source-text features by introducing other features elsewhere in the target text — features not necessarily present in the source — in order to balance the information load or make the style more consistent overall.

Hervey et al. describe four types of compensation: in kind (replace one feature type with another, e.g. German infinitive instructions with English imperatives, or add stylistic devices to recreate a level of formality), in place (recreate a lost effect at a different point in the text), by splitting (spell out a source word that has no single equivalent, e.g. 'fastener' as bolts, screws, clips), and by merging (condense a long stretch or compound into a shorter phrase or single word).

Information in a technical text is usually presented in a logical or chronological sequence — especially in instructional or process texts, in the order in which it is required and fairly stable because it tracks real-world objects or processes — but there are instances where cultural expectations and norms take priority and the sequence must be rearranged.

To produce effective translations a translator may need to alter the sequencing and even the proportion of given and new information within paragraphs or sections — by foregrounding, omitting, or repeating information — because different languages favour different given/new ordering relative to the reader's assumed background knowledge (Gerzymisch-Arbogast).

The structure of a document may need to be changed for different language audiences (Ulijn): what is perceived as the most logical sequence of information for one audience can be counterintuitive or confusing for another, as with a table of contents reordered for a different readership.

A translator may rearrange information within sentences, paragraphs, or even chapters, but must not move entire chapters or sections within a document without permission, because that is not really the translator's job; at minimum the client should be informed.
exception: reordering whole chapters or sections requires the client's permission

statement: Poorly written source texts may present information in the wrong order even for the source-language audience (for example, instructions that tell readers to delete a file before backing it up), which may require the translator to rearrange the information.
condition: source text is poorly sequenced

statement: Iconic Linkage improves usability by reducing the number of ways the same information is presented: it extends parallelism from nearby phrases to matching sentences across an entire text, so when the source expresses the same information several times with slightly different wording, the translator should pick one single translation and use it for all occurrences.

Research indicates Iconic Linkage significantly improves a text's effectiveness by minimizing the cognitive effort and problem-solving needed to understand it and by improving predictability and aiding learning through habit formation; it is nearly always good to translate the same information the same way, which improves clarity, consistency, and professionalism and makes translation memory more effective for pivot or relay translations.

Perhaps the single most important factor in how to approach a translation is the type of translation the client actually wants, because it determines what is translated, how it is translated, and how much time is spent doing it.

Translations vary by purpose with different quality expectations: a selective translation renders only certain sections; a gist translation is a rough summary needing less care over style and register; an information-purposes translation must convey all the information but tolerates rough style for internal use; and a publication-purposes translation demands the best possible content and flawless language and style, often with a second translator or reviewer.

In update projects — translating a revised version of a previously translated document, often with a supplied translation memory — professional ethics and good business sense favour telling the client that only a proportion of the text needs translating rather than charging for the whole.
condition: translation is an update of a previously translated document

statement: In update projects, existing translations proposed by the translation memory should generally be accepted as is and previously translated sentences left unedited — because they have already been client-approved and any change has a knock-on effect on other translations derived from them — so translate only the new sections, replicating the existing style and tone; but if a previous translation is downright wrong, raise it with the client, preferably before changing anything.
condition: reusing an approved translation memory on an update
exception: a previous translation that is downright wrong should be flagged to the client

statement: An instrumental translation (Nord) is used in place of the source text and is expected to perform as a freestanding, autonomous target-language text, so any errors must be corrected for it to perform its intended function.
condition: instrumental translations

statement: A documentary translation (Nord) describes what was said in the source and how it was said and is used for back-translations that check a translation's quality or for judicial purposes where liability rests on exact wording; in this mode errors are not corrected but shown — and back-translation is a questionable, very limited way of assessing translation quality.
condition: documentary translations and back-translations

statement: In an instrumental translation the translator, as the expert, should correct without hesitation simple linguistic errors (spelling mistakes, typos, unclear formulations), unclear descriptions and instructions, incorrect line breaks, mismatches between paragraph text and diagrams, and obviously wrong units of measure (for example a '250 kg' children's paracetamol tablet where 'kg' should be 'mg').
condition: instrumental translations

statement: The translation brief that Skopos theory relies on has no settled form and remains open to interpretation; because clients often do not supply the needed information, translators frequently have to work from a system of educated guesses and assumptions.

Compile a short list of standard questions to ask the client at the start of a project, but keep the number small: too many questions can irritate a client and be read as a lack of professionalism, and in most cases the translator is the expert who is expected to 'just know' how to translate the material.

The very minimum a translator should establish before a project is the target language variety (e.g. UK vs US English), the purpose of the translation (information vs publication), the deadline, and whether any specific terminology must be used.
Not all of the text in a technical document necessarily needs to be translated: certain parts either should not be translated at all or should be translated only in certain circumstances.

When a technical text quotes another publication, do not simply translate it as a direct quote (which risks being taken as the actual words of the original); first establish whether an authoritative published translation of the referenced document already exists in the target language, and if it exists and can be obtained, use it rather than your own translation.
condition: the source text quotes from another publication

statement: If no authoritative translation of a quoted document exists or can be obtained, present a paraphrase translation that explains the content without purporting to be the official text — either omit the quote where the document permits, or give the original source-language text accompanied by your paraphrase in square brackets to mark it as supplementary information not in the original.
condition: no authoritative translation of the quoted material is available

statement: When a text references a named law, keep the reference tied to the correct jurisdiction — for example a reference to a German law must remain about that German law and not another country's law that happens to share the same name.
condition: references to named laws

statement: For EU-related texts translated between official EU languages, almost all terminology, official names, and associated documentation have already been translated into the official languages, so consulting the relevant EU website (such as EUR-Lex) yields the correct authoritative translation.
condition: translating between official EU languages

statement: An EU directive is a legislative act that requires member states to achieve a particular result by a specified deadline without prescribing how, and is named by both a short reference (year/identifier/abbreviation, e.g. 85/337/EEC) and a longer descriptive name findable in the EUR-Lex directory of legislation in force.

The abbreviation in an EU directive's short reference code differs from language to language (for 2003/35: EC in English, EG in German, ES in Czech, EY in Finnish, EF in Danish, EK in Greek, KE in Maltese, CE in Spanish and French), so the translator must select the version with the correct short code for the target language and must not leave the codes unchanged.
condition: translating the names of EU directives

statement: A controlled language (CL) is a subset of a natural language whose rules restrict the grammar and vocabulary allowed, to reduce ambiguity and complexity; human-oriented controlled languages (e.g. ASD Simplified Technical English) improve readability for people, while machine-oriented controlled languages make texts easier for computers to process, such as for machine translation.

A source text written in a controlled language may be easier to understand and translate, but being required to translate into a controlled language may force the translator to completely recast sentences within a limited range of grammatical and lexical options to conform, sometimes enforced by computerized style checkers.
condition: translating into a controlled language

statement: A style guide is a set of standards, less strict than a controlled language, governing how documents are written and presented for consistency and comprehensibility (often for non-native readers); it may specify grammatical constructions, sentence structure, preferred terminology, punctuation, how to address the reader, how to phrase headings, and how to refer to products.

Even a source-language style guide can be useful to the translator (for example on the correct use of product names), and a style guide may require the translator to modify an initial translation choice to comply with its rules on matters such as tense, direct speech, or preferred terms.

Typical technical style-guide rules include: use the second person to address the user directly, do not use the possessive form of product names, use the present tense, use positive constructions where possible, use consistent terminology, use gerunds rather than infinitive verb forms in headings, and avoid anthropomorphism.

Terminology is generally the least problematic part of a technical translation given access to the Internet and good dictionaries; when it does cause problems, the cause is usually people and factors outside the text rather than what the terms actually mean.

Large companies often mandate preferred terminology — sometimes with collocation rules (e.g. cancel but not abort a process, run but not execute a program) to avoid unwanted connotations or unnecessary variation — so the most logical-seeming translation of a term is not necessarily the one required, and the translator should accommodate the client's wishes even when the rules seem counterintuitive.
condition: client mandates preferred terminology

statement: The translator must be notified of any terminological or stylistic preferences at the start of a job and be given the right resources (style guides, glossaries); a client cannot reasonably complain that a translation fails to use their terminology if they did not supply clear instructions or the necessary resources.

As a general rule, check the customer's website to get a feel for how they write their documents, even when they have no specific language requirements, so the translation has the look and feel of one of the client's own documents and increases client satisfaction.

Readability has traditionally been measured with tests such as Flesch Reading Ease (0–100, higher meaning more readable), Flesch-Kincaid (mapping that score onto a US school grade level), the Fog Index, and Fry's graph, which analyze factors like word count, average sentence length, and the number of polysyllabic words, but such tests are language-specific.

Texts can be made more readable by keeping sentences as short as possible and using simple sentence structures and words, but readability is not the whole picture: a readable text is not necessarily a good or effective one, which is why the emphasis has shifted from readability to usability.

Usability of a document is how well a reader can read it, understand it, and perform the required task or remember the required information effectively and efficiently, and how satisfied or unstressed they are afterward; a usable text gives the right information, in the right proportions, at the right time, and in the right format.

Strategies to make a translated text more usable: use terminology consistently and avoid polysemy, use clear and simple language, write instructions in chronological order, use direct and active language, do not provide unnecessary information (avoid over-using expansion), implement Iconic Linkage, and keep the number of tenses to a minimum.

A golden rule of translation is never to return a translation without first running a spellchecker and reading through the text one last time yourself, because a spellchecker only finds misspelled words, not correctly spelled words that are the wrong words (it will not flag 'wit hall' where you meant 'with all').

When revising another translator's work, the task is to find and fix errors, not to rewrite the translation so it looks like your own: check that all information is translated correctly and accurately, that terminology is correct and consistent, that the style suits the text type and audience, and that spelling, orthography, and punctuation are correct — and do not replace something that is correct just because you prefer a different phrasing or term.
condition: revising or editing another translator's work

statement: When editing and reviewing, provide two copies (a tracked-changes copy with comments for the translator and a clean copy for the client), distance yourself from the text before editing to gain fresh eyes, stay objective and constructive (briefly explain each change, avoid sarcasm), and do not use proofreading to impose your own style — changes must be a genuine improvement, not a matter of personal preference.
condition: editing and reviewing translations

statement: Do not use footnotes in a professional translation to flag your confusion or queries: because there is no guarantee the translation will be reviewed before publication, such footnotes can reach the end reader, expose your confusion, undermine your credibility, and deface the text; annotated translations with explanatory footnotes are only a student learning aid.
exception: annotated translations used as a student learning exercise

statement: Instead of footnotes, keep a record of your queries as you go (including the page number and the source sentence or word), send minor queries with the final delivery and serious ones by email while working, phrase them as clearly and concisely as possible, and refer to them in the cover email so a busy project manager does not miss them.

Acronyms and abbreviations are used for brevity and to avoid repeating the same words, and can be grouped by referent (international organizations, national organizations, company names, and so on), each posing potential problems for readers and translators depending on their nature and context.

Acronyms and abbreviations can be handled by one of several strategies: transfer (keep the source acronym if well known), reconstitute (translate the full name and build a new target acronym, for non-specialized or ad-hoc acronyms), define (replace with a definition when it cannot be transcribed or reconstituted, useful for Latin abbreviations), combine (transfer plus definition, done once at first use), write out the source-language full name (for higher-level texts whose audience knows the source culture), and translate (use an official or widely used translated name and its acronym if they exist).

In the vast majority of cases equations do not need to be modified by the translator and can be left untouched or copied and pasted; still, knowing that formulae can be rearranged to make another variable the subject, and that equations may be embedded as images or inserted via special characters, ASCII codes, or an equation editor, helps the translator follow the text and reproduce any symbols that appear in running sentences or in a hardcopy source.

Be careful with variable symbols used inside ordinary paragraph text, because similar-looking symbols (such as R and the Greek rho, or the micro sign and the letter u) are easily confused; a safe approach is to copy and paste the symbol from elsewhere in the text or from a parallel text rather than retyping it.
If you cannot tell what a particular symbol is, change the font, which can reveal that two characters that looked identical are actually different (for example a letter 'I' versus the digit '1').

Converting precise quantities from one system of units to another can be problematic, costly, or even dangerous, because the translator may not know how precise the rounding needs to be — in fields such as chemistry there can be a significant difference between, for example, 1.06 mg and 1.1 mg.

SI prefixes indicate multiples (e.g. kilo = 1000) or divisions (e.g. milli = one thousandth) of a base unit, and confusion arises from unfamiliarity with prefix meanings, from similar-sounding prefixes such as deci- and deca-, and from prefix symbols such as the micro sign being confused with the letter u.

The most common and safest strategy for units of measure is to leave them unchanged, particularly SI quantities, because it ensures accuracy and prevents translator-induced error; this is especially valid for a specialist audience who will know the units or be able to convert them.

In user-oriented texts it is almost always better to address the reader directly as 'you' rather than as 'the user', because it is clearer and leaves less room for misunderstanding — unless the target audience has a very strong aversion to direct address.
exception: target audience strongly averse to direct address or informality

statement: Humour does not travel: a golden rule of technical communication is that technical texts should not contain humour, jokes, or anything silly, so work on the assumption that jokes will not cross into the target text and remove them; if unsure about removing humour, mention it to the client and explain it is not appropriate and probably would not be funny anyway.

Content that congratulates the user for purchasing a product, common in some consumer manuals, may be regarded in other cultures as insincere flattery that is irritating and patronizing, so the translator should exercise common sense about whether it is appropriate for the target audience.

If humour must be retained, ensure it is appropriate for the audience, subject, and text type; and in texts such as popular science, where a joke may exist for a reason (to illustrate a concept or scenario), the rendering should fulfil that function, using a non-humorous means if humour cannot.
condition: when humour must be kept because it serves a function

statement: Translating into a language that favours 'you' over 'the user' does not license being overly familiar, using slang, or treating the reader as a friend — it is still technical documentation.

Different languages may approach and describe the same concepts from completely different angles, so the translator should not let the particular phrasing of a source term or description overly influence the translation.

Source texts can often contain errors — 'living texts are faulty texts' (Honig) — ranging from simple spelling mistakes to serious factual mistakes, and how they are handled depends as much on the translator and the intended purpose as on the error itself.

The key decision on source-text errors — correct them or preserve them — reduces to whether the job is an instrumental or a documentary translation, so the translator should find out from the client which is needed, being persistent and ready to explain the distinction in simple terms since clients usually do not know it.
condition: source text contains errors

statement: Subject-related (factual) errors are the trickiest category because detecting them depends on the translator's own subject knowledge; some standards, such as Germany's DIN 2345, relieve the translator of responsibility for source errors by placing it on the client, who is responsible for resolving errors and answering the translator's questions.

When a translator spots what looks like an error in the source text, they should notify the client, and decide — based on the text's length, subject, and deadline — whether to raise queries as they go (important on large or multi-translator projects, where an answer may be needed before continuing) or to compile them and send them on delivery, according to the client's preference.

Handle source errors by type: correct simple linguistic errors (misspellings, punctuation, awkward language) quietly; refer completely incomprehensible meaning back to the client; correct minor factual errors (e.g. a text saying distance is measured in kilograms) but at least notify the client; and even for a serious error you are certain of and can fix, still contact the client for clarification.
condition: instrumental translation where errors are to be fixed

statement: A translation for publication purposes is generally instrumental (so errors should be fixed), but the converse does not hold: an information-purposes text cannot be assumed to be a documentary translation.

Translators are not expected to be programmers, but they are expected to recognize program code and know how to handle it in a translation, and they are often responsible in localization projects for translating the text displayed on screen in software or on a website.

Recognizing code is hard when translating from English because commands and arguments resemble English words (verbose, print, return, getName, IF, FOR, WHILE); useful clues are that words written entirely in uppercase, and multi-word tokens joined without spaces or by underscores (e.g. MENUITEM, Style_Caption), are usually non-translatable object identifiers that should be left unchanged.
condition: texts documenting or containing program code

statement: In software localization, some punctuated strings still need translating: menu strings contain ampersands to mark hotkeys (e.g. &View, F&ormat), so the translator must not delete the ampersands, must pay attention to their placement within the word, must not add a space immediately after them, and must ensure the resulting hotkeys are unique.
condition: localizing software menu strings with hotkeys

statement: Variables act as placeholders (usually preceded by $ or %, e.g. '$d results', '%1') and impose a syntax the translation must accommodate: where a string contains two identical variables (e.g. 'Click %s to update %s'), the translator must preserve the order of the variables and rework the translation around it, or the runtime substitution will be wrong.
condition: strings containing runtime variables

statement: Plurals generated by variables can restrict phrasing where a language lacks a consistent plural marker; Esselink recommends deleting such plural variables and replacing them with a translation that represents both singular and plural forms (e.g. batch(es)), but the translator should exercise caution with code and variables and consult the client or project manager when in doubt.
condition: strings whose plurals are generated by variables

statement: Commented-out text in code (preceded by symbols such as //, /*, {, #, * or enclosed in comment tags) gives programmers information, is not displayed in the finished product, and therefore does not need to be translated — except in rare cases such as sample files or training materials where you are explicitly asked to.
exception: sample files or training materials where translating comments is explicitly requested

statement: Rules for translating around code: do not assume everything must be translated; do not translate underscore-joined or single-word compounds (e.g. CompanyName, File_Description); text in quotation marks usually needs translating, but quoted proper nouns such as font, variable, or interface-element names (e.g. 'scrollbar') should be left untranslated; preserve trailing ellipses (Print...) and trailing spaces inside quotes (used to concatenate strings); do not delete, modify, or rearrange variables; beware single-word strings like 'None' that may have gender-dependent translations; and ensure your translation matches the text that actually appears in the software.
condition: translating text that contains program code or software strings

statement: Diagrams should ideally use numbered labels; word labels are problematic when the diagram is inserted as a picture, since translating them requires a graphics editor and re-import (which is not strictly the translator's job), so a good solution is to supply the label translations in a three-column table rather than editing the image.
condition: diagrams with textual labels embedded as images

statement: Product and brand names should always be written the same way and never modified even when they look funny, ungrammatical, or wrong (e.g. SharePoint, InDesign, Kia cee'd), because they are proper names central to the product's identity and to its copyright protection, which is based on a particular spelling or orthographic presentation.

When a text names a specific brand of a material or product (e.g. a stent in a surgery paper or an antifreeze in a car manual), it is usually mentioned for a reason, so transfer the name to the target text without modification; if the product is internationally recognized or available in the target country, transcribe the name exactly as it appears in the source.
condition: text names a specific brand for a reason

statement: If a brand is non-existent or unknown in the target-language culture, do not simply replace it with a comparable target brand, because the two products — though similar — may differ in characteristics, properties, or chemical composition, which in a chemistry paper could have significant implications for the repeatability or even the safety of the study, so research the products first.
condition: brand named in the source is unknown in the target culture

statement: Handle an unknown brand by text type: in specialist texts where a product's precise characteristics matter, reproduce the brand name and add a brief phrase describing its function; in general texts, replace it with a comparable product (qualified with 'such as' to avoid implying the client endorses it) or, ideally, a generic description — but only after researching the product to ensure the substitute really is equivalent.
condition: substituting or describing a brand unknown in the target culture

statement: For contact names where gender is unclear to the target reader, add the title Mr. or Ms. as a value-added service; and never translate email or website addresses (translating them breaks the address or sends readers to wrong-language content) — leave them as they are and instead notify the client, suggesting suitable target-language alternatives.

Convert all telephone numbers to international format with dialling codes and prefixes (e.g. 051-1234567 to +353-(0)51-1234567) since the translation will be read outside the source country, and identify mobile numbers because callers may incur international charges; for postal addresses, do not assume readers know the source country's geography — add the country, or an international prefix to the post code (e.g. LT-03500 Vilnius, B-1000 Brussels), when the country is not identified.

Replace culture-specific and context-based examples (geographical, commercial, external) with scenarios familiar to the target audience; language-specific examples may require significant adaptation or entirely new examples; and examples constrained by technical factors usually need only minimal modification because the technical context stays the same, unless there is language-specificity or different technical regulations apply.

When technical accuracy and linguistic fluency conflict — as with a text carrying an encoded or hidden message — the translator should prioritize the technical, factual aspect over the linguistic; the balance depends on the text and subject, but the technical will usually need to take priority.
condition: when full technical accuracy and full linguistic fluency cannot both be achieved

statement: Translating warning and advisory information clearly and effectively is extremely important — in some cases a matter of life or death — both to keep readers from harm and for legal reasons, so warnings deserve particular care.

Notices follow a severity hierarchy — Note (reminds of or emphasizes important information or minor problems), Warning (possible minor injury to people), Caution (possible damage to equipment, data, or other significant consequences), and Danger (possible serious or fatal injury) — and it is as important not to overstate risk as to understate it: understating means readers do not take a risk seriously, while overstating (using Danger where Warning fits) lessens the impact of Danger when it is truly warranted.

The EU has standardized hazard symbols (each on an orange background with an explanatory text description) whose descriptions are already translated into most official EU languages, so the translator should use those official translated descriptions wherever the language combination permits.
condition: hazard labelling in EU official languages

statement: References to other documents can be handled by paraphrasing (replace the source name with a descriptive phrase when its precise name is unimportant), retaining (keep the source name when it is important but its meaning is unimportant or clear from context), or retaining and paraphrasing (keep the name plus a descriptive paraphrase — in sentence or, for bullet lists, in square brackets — when the name matters but its meaning is not obvious), so the reader both understands it and can still identify the source text.
condition: references to other named documents

statement: For academic publications it is generally unnecessary to translate the names of referenced documents, since they normally appear only in the bibliography and rarely in the body text; however, author and publication names may need transliterating when translating between different writing systems.
condition: academic publications

statement: Scientific papers frequently arrive partially translated, because authors who speak the target language try to help by rendering individual words, phrases, or whole paragraphs themselves; this is well-intentioned but the translator must still take responsibility for handling and reconciling those pre-translated parts.

Linnaean classification is a standard binomial nomenclatural system in scientific discourse that assigns each organism a unique two-part Latin name (genus then species, e.g. Corydoras paleatus), and Latin is likewise used in medical contexts for anatomical terms of location and directional terms.

Scientific nomenclature is valuable because every species is uniquely named, the names are understood by experts across countries and languages, spelling and punctuation are consistent, and — being revisable only by expert committees — the names are stable and do not gain connotations; the translator can therefore either leave the Latin terms unchanged or use the standard international term to locate the commonly used target-language equivalent.

Handle Latin scientific terms by one of three strategies: retain (usually best, as it identifies the concept accurately — print Latin terms in italics), explain (use the Latin term to identify the common target-language name and include it in parentheses or an explanatory phrase when the target audience lacks the source audience's background, as in a medical article for a general audience or a patient information sheet), or replace (substitute the common target-language name where the target audience or language has had no exposure to Latin and the terms would only confuse).
condition: translating Latin scientific or anatomical terminology

statement: To find a Latin term's target-language meaning, search for the Latin term together with a related target-language word (enclosing phrases in quotes); if it returns no results the term may be misspelled, so use a search engine's suggested spelling or search a shorter fragment or a fuzzy variant.

If a set of instructions does not make sense or you cannot figure out what is being described, contact the client and ask them to walk you through the process; do not translate instructions you do not understand.
condition: instructions in the source are unclear or nonsensical

statement: A reliable way to test instructions is to have someone follow them literally, using no common sense, initiative, or problem-solving, which exposes weaknesses in how the information is explained; instructions should be calibrated to the likely audience — not so detailed that they patronize, nor so sparse that they confuse.

Do not translate a table of contents first or in place: auto-generated tables of contents are a projection of the actual heading text located elsewhere in the document, so a translation typed into the TOC itself is lost when the document is printed or updated — you must instead translate the real heading text that is projected into it.
condition: auto-generated tables of contents

statement: Because section headings describe the content of their sections, translating a table of contents before reading and translating those sections risks mistranslating the headings for lack of context; it is best to leave the table of contents until the rest of the text has been translated.

Indexes are also auto-generated, and translating the index first to use as a glossary carries the same risk of translating terms out of context — you may pick the wrong term, discover it mid-translation, and have to go back and fix every instance — so be very cautious about doing so.

Technical translation is often subject to strict space constraints — single-sheet leaflets, software interface character limits for dialog strings, and diagram or graph labels — and because a translation naturally expands or contracts depending on the language combination and direction (sometimes significantly), the translator may have to rethink strategies to fit the available space.

To fit strict space constraints: use short, simple words and sentences; use clear abbreviations (preferably ones already used by the company or subject area, without overusing them); deviate from the source structure where a different target grammar produces a shorter rendering; use imperative verb forms, which are shorter and easier to understand than passives; and be flexible and creative with modulation, transposition, and adaptation.
condition: translating under strict space constraints

statement: Manage project files by creating a folder per project and always keeping a copy of the source files in a separate folder, preferably on a separate drive, computer, or online storage, so that a crash or corruption does not force you to ask the client to resend the files; set up daily backups to a separate location.

When translating a file you are generally expected to overwrite the source text with your translation, using the source as a template so the formatting matches exactly (not for PDFs, which cannot be edited normally, and never by retyping into a blank document); never work on the only copy — save it under a new name in the target folder first; and give translated files unique, identifiable names by keeping the original filename and appending the ISO target-language code (e.g. specification-doc-2010_ZH.doc for Chinese).
exception: PDF files, which cannot be edited like normal documents

statement: Parallel texts are one of the most useful resources for a translator, explaining the subject and providing terminology; because certain document types are typically published in a particular format (manuals, reports, and specifications as PDF, marketing as HTML or PDF, training material as PowerPoint), a translator can use a search engine's advanced format filter to find suitable parallel texts.

Search operators speed up translation research: a tilde before a term finds synonyms, a minus sign (or the NOT operator) excludes unwanted pages, and searching a source-language term together with a related target-language word surfaces bilingual pages likely to contain a translation or glossary.

Translator forums let you draw on other translators' expertise, but rely on their answers with extreme caution: there is no mechanism ensuring answer quality, you (who do not know the answer) must judge which is correct, and answerers may not know your full context and may give an answer that is right in one situation but wrong in another.

Assess online source reliability by rules of thumb: international-organization, government, and state websites are usually reliable (limit searches with the government domain suffix); company websites are less objective but good for terminology, and a localized company site gives a ready bilingual resource; supposedly impartial review sites may be slanted; personal or free-hosted sites are the least reliable; and Wikipedia should never be relied on alone — use it only as a first port of call and corroborate any information with other sources, because vandalism can persist for hours.

Addition (related to explicitation) is the translation procedure of adding extra information to a text during translation, motivated by factors such as the clarity and comprehensibility of the target text, legal requirements, or political, cultural, and social influences.

House distinguishes covert translation — functionally equivalent to the source and not obviously a translation, as though it had been written in the target language — from overt translation, where it is evident the target text is a translation.

A locale is, in computing, the set of parameters defining a user's language, country, and special variant preferences to be reflected in software, and more generally all the linguistic, cultural, geographic, technical, and political factors that identify a particular target audience.

A pivot (relay or indirect) translation is one where, when no translator is available for a language combination, the text is first translated into an intermediate language and then into the desired target language (e.g. German to English to Japanese).

An overt translation (House) is one where the source text's function is not maintained and the text is not functionally equivalent: the target audience is overtly not being addressed and it is obvious the text is a translation, usually because the source is inextricably linked to a specific time, culture, or language — the contrast to a covert translation.

The purpose of a text (its ultimate intended use, as in Skopos theory — e.g. to let a client file a patent application or to let engineers understand a technology) should not be confused with its function (the effect the text has on its audience or the way it interacts with them).

Internationally standardized Hazard, Risk (R-phrases), and Safety (S-phrases) set phrases exist for dangerous materials, with authoritative official translations in a range of European languages published in the Official Journal of the European Communities (O.J. L 225/1); these approved set phrases should always be used when translating safety information rather than translating the wording freely.
condition: translating hazard, risk, and safety information for dangerous materials

statement: Some unit names are ambiguous across locales and must be handled with care: the 'ton' can be the metric tonne (1000 kg), the UK long ton (about 1020 kg), or the US short ton (about 907 kg), so a translator must identify which is meant before rendering or converting it.
condition: units whose meaning differs by country or system
